overview: Picture a giant royal umbrella folding while dozens of smaller umbrellas pop open beneath it. Around 1000 CE, the Gurjara-Pratihara court still claimed Kannauj, but its great ninth-century empire had already lost powerful lords, forts and provinces. Mahmud of Ghazni raided Kannauj in 1018; Rajyapala fled and was killed after a Chandela-led response. Trilochanapala then issued a copper grant near Prayaga in 1027, and a Yashapala inscription dated 1036 may mark a last flicker, though that family link is disputed. The atlas makes the puzzle stranger: its separate id pratiharas runs from 1000 to 1200, misses Kannauj, Gwalior and Jhusi, and stretches east across Gorakhpur and Patna. This card follows the historical line only to its cautious early-eleventh-century ending, then explains the people, temples, farms, markets and successor powers that continued. Inscriptions favor kings and donors, so gaps about children, healers and toilets are labeled instead of filled with guesses.

periods.title: Rajyapala rules a much smaller Kannauj realm
periods.summary: The imperial network had already contracted as Chandelas, Kachchhapaghatas, Paramaras and other regional powers acted independently. Rajyapala still held Kannauj, but old royal titles did not restore ninth-century reach.

periods.title: Kannauj is raided and Rajyapala is killed
periods.summary: Mahmud of Ghazni entered Kannauj in 1018 after Rajyapala withdrew. Chandela evidence says a coalition punished Rajyapala soon afterward, revealing both the shock of invasion and his weak authority among former subordinates.

periods.title: Trilochanapala survives east of the old capital
periods.summary: Trilochanapala appears after Rajyapala and is securely documented by a Sanskrit copper plate dated 26 June 1027 near Prayaga. The record shows a royal household and grant machinery continuing in reduced territory.

periods.title: A disputed last trace at Kara
periods.summary: A 1036 inscription at Kara records a grant by Yashapala in Kausambi-mandala. Older histories often call him the last Pratihara, but the surviving text does not securely prove his relationship to the imperial line.

periods.title: The imperial state disappears, not its countryside
periods.summary: After the last possible royal traces, no continuous Pratihara empire can be demonstrated. Kalachuri and Pala competition reached the middle Ganges, while farms, shrines, routes and local authorities continued under changing rulers.

periods.title: Former core lands belong to competing courts
periods.summary: Kannauj and Varanasi sat in a contested landscape rather than a surviving Pratihara block. The atlas still waits until 1200 to remove pratiharas, so its broad label now diverges sharply from political chronology.

periods.title: Gahadavala power rises around Kannauj and Varanasi
periods.summary: Chandradeva and later Gahadavala rulers established a different dynasty in much of the former Pratihara heartland. Their rise belongs to successor context and must not be silently relabeled as continued Pratihara rule.

periods.title: A crowded regional world reaches the atlas seam
periods.summary: Chauhans, Chandelas, Palas, Senas, Gahadavalas and other powers shaped northern India before Ghurid victories. At 1200 the atlas replaces its Pratihara layer, but that seam is not a two-century imperial fall date.

sections.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake

items.text: The exact imported record is id “pratiharas,” name “Pratiharas,” circa 1000 to 1200. The earlier id gurjara-pratihara is separately indexed from 800 to 1000 and already has its own card. This bundle creates a standalone continuation card; it does not alias, replace or duplicate that earlier record.

At 1000 the target is one Polygon, one ring and 29 positions. Its bounds are 77.061° to 94.154° east and 25.106° to 32.309° north; coordinate SHA-256 is 610039ec6650844e94ac104e78125ae6df7620a406eca047ffb2bc94e7f416b3. Ayodhya, Gorakhpur and Patna test inside, while Kannauj and Gwalior do not.

At 1100 the polygon remains one ring but changes to 31 positions, bounds 77.061° to 94.370° east and 25.105° to 32.309° north, SHA-256 936e72e00c7635bc64be188b5fa2fc5341c63ab8bc0e16884b5e0d7958d1959f. It still contains Ayodhya, Gorakhpur and Patna while excluding Kannauj, Gwalior, Prayaga, Jhusi and Kara.

The 1000 polygon overlaps rajput-kingdoms at Ayodhya and Gorakhpur and overlaps palas at Patna. At 1100, the atlas gives Kannauj and Varanasi to chandellas, Gwalior to its misspelled paramas layer, and Patna solely to pratiharas. These graphics cannot be read as clean or mutually exclusive frontiers.

At 700 the exact target is absent. At 800 and 900, the earlier gurjara-pratihara polygon includes Kannauj, Gwalior and major western or central centers. At 1200, pratiharas disappears and broad Delhi Sultanate and rajput-kingdoms layers take over many tests. The abrupt eastward jump at 1000 is a data-model break, not measured territorial history.

sections.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins

items.text: Pratihara histories begin with more than one branch and several debated origin stories. Inscriptions linked the royal family to Lakshmana, Rama’s brother and legendary door guardian. Historians treat that genealogy as political prestige, not a birth certificate reaching back into an epic age.

The label “Gurjara-Pratihara” has generated modern arguments about ethnicity, region and dynasty. One late subordinate inscription uses the compound explicitly, while imperial records vary. A careful card preserves the historical name without pretending that one word identifies every subject’s ancestry or a modern community unchanged across twelve centuries.

Nagabhata II captured Kannauj, and Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala later ruled the dynasty at its height. Competition with Pala and Rashtrakuta rulers is often called a tripartite struggle, but campaigns, alliances and regional lords changed repeatedly. A triangle on a school diagram should not become three permanent colored teams.

Imperial government depended on subordinate rulers, officers, landed beneficiaries and local communities. Kings could proclaim universal power, yet practical control varied by road, fort, town and season. When strong lords stopped cooperating, the empire contracted without every plough, workshop or shrine waiting for a single command from Kannauj.

The earlier gurjara-pratihara card covers the high imperial phase from 800 to 1000. This target begins at an atlas seam just when the historical empire was weakest. Its job is therefore to connect the last Kannauj rulers to that predecessor while refusing to stretch their government all the way to 1200.

sections.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036

items.text: Rajyapala ruled Kannauj as former feudatories controlled much of the older empire. Mahmud of Ghazni’s 1018 campaign reached the city, and accounts differ on whether Rajyapala fled or submitted. Either way, the episode shows a vulnerable court; it does not prove that every community in northern India suddenly changed rulers that morning.

Chandela records celebrate Rajyapala’s killing after the raid and credit Arjuna, a subordinate of the Chandela ruler. This is evidence of a coalition policing royal honor and exploiting weakness. It is also victory writing, so the exact motives and choreography cannot be recovered as if an eyewitness filmed the meeting.

The 1027 Jhusi plate names Trilochanapala after Rajyapala and Vijayapala and gives him very grand titles. It was issued on the Ganges near Prayaga, far from a restored continent-sized empire. Magnificent titles could travel on a shrinking royal letterhead; geography and effective power still require separate evidence.

The Kara gateway inscription dated 1036 records Yashapala granting Payalasa village in Kausambi-mandala to Mathura Vikata of Pabhosa, with customary dues, royalties, taxes, gold and tithes. It is an unusually late administrative glimpse, but whether this Yashapala certainly belonged to the imperial Pratihara family remains debated.

By the later eleventh century, records place Kalachuri and then Gahadavala rulers around Varanasi and Kannauj. The Pratihara political ending was a fragmentation and replacement, not a vanishing population. Farmers, merchants, ritual specialists, artisans and scribes continued while royal names above them changed.

sections.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory

items.text: Pratihara rule worked through layered relationships. A royal court recognized regional lords; those lords sponsored temples and managed local forces; village elites and corporate groups handled resources on the ground. The system could expand quickly through alliances, but the same structure let powerful subordinates become independent when the center weakened.

Gwalior’s 876 inscription names cultivators Dallaka and Memmaka and describes two fields by the amount of barley seed needed to sow them. Boundaries used rocks, another field and a water channel. Grand endowments still needed neighbors to know exactly which patch of dirt the elegant Sanskrit meant.

Pehowa’s 882 record describes horse dealers contributing fees to maintain temples at Pehowa and Kannauj. Merchants, animals, toll-like payments and religious institutions met in one organized arrangement. It reveals administration through a commercial community, not simply royal tax collectors appearing everywhere with identical forms.

Royal grants were social instructions as well as documents. Courts depended on ranked officers, village leaders, landholders and recipients to recognize new rights and obligations locally. A copper plate could announce authority, but its commands still had to be understood, remembered and enforced by people on the ground.

Yashapala’s possible last grant was made to an individual rather than securely identified as a Brahmana religious gift. Historians have read it as a service grant, perhaps to a literate Kayastha official, but that social identification is an inference. The inscription securely gives the grantee’s name, place and revenue package.

sections.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs

items.text: Pratihara rulers had fought Palas in the east and Rashtrakutas in the Deccan for influence around Kannauj. Those wars were not one continuous three-way match. Kings died, branches split, feudatories shifted sides and campaigns followed routes and forts; large zones of claimed authority contained communities with very different local histories.

The 1018 invasion tied north Indian politics to Ghazni, but the response was also deeply regional. Chandela power, a Gwalior subordinate and the diminished Kannauj court all mattered. “Foreign invasion” and “internal rivalry” were happening together, which is why one arrow on a map cannot explain Rajyapala’s fall.

After the Pratiharas, Kalachuris, Chandelas and Gahadavalas competed in the Ganges-Yamuna region. Farther west, Chauhans, Paramaras, Chaulukyas and other houses had their own courts. These were not obedient pieces waiting to reunite; each formed alliances, patronized institutions and claimed status for itself.

Premodern power often followed nodes, roads, river crossings and negotiated relationships rather than a surveyed line. That model fits the inscriptions better than the atlas’s polygon reaching almost to 94° east. A royal title at one camp or a land grant in one district cannot fill every pixel between them.

No single atlas successor matches the Pratihara dissolution. At 1200, Delhi Sultanate and rajput-kingdoms polygons absorb many tested points, while Chandelas, Chauhans and Palas have separate indexed histories. The structured ending therefore names no one-to-one successor, even though the target records a predecessor link to gurjara-pratihara.

sections.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving

items.text: The Gwalior endowment required oil workers and guild leaders from several towns to provide measured oil from every press each month for temple lamps. A glowing shrine depended on crushing seed, maintaining presses, measuring liquid and organizing deliveries. The miracle here was partly a dependable supply schedule.

A rock inscription from about 942 to 943 credits Vinayakapala with irrigation work on the Urvasi River and names Bhailadaman, son of Krishnaraja, as writer. Water engineering involved embankments or channels, labor and maintenance; public memory also required somebody trained to compose and write the record.

Early medieval northern farms produced wheat, barley, rice, millets, pulses, sesame, mustard, sugarcane, cotton and other crops in different ecological zones. This list describes regional possibilities, not one family’s dinner or one village’s field. Rain, rivers, wells and local soils decided what could actually grow.

Trade joined market towns, pilgrimage places and rural producers. Horse dealers at Pehowa are unusually visible, while other merchants moved salt, cloth, grain, oil, metal goods and ritual supplies. Historians debate whether every early medieval town declined, so the card avoids both a golden-age bazaar and an empty-city myth.

A debased silver Gurjara-Pratihara coin in the British Museum weighs 3.18 grams and imitates an older Indo-Sasanian design: a rough ruler bust on one face and a fire altar with attendant on the other. Long-lived imagery made money recognizable even when the portrait would never win a drawing contest.

sections.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero

items.text: At Gwalior, officer Alla commissioned the Caturbhuj temple under Mihira Bhoja. Workers cut its interior from living rock rather than stacking every wall. The inscription ties architecture to a named official, while the finished space points to planners, quarrying skill, tool makers, stone cutters and many laborers the text leaves unnamed.

Pratihara-style temples experimented with plans, wall projections, doorways, towers and sculpture as temple building expanded across early medieval India. The tall Teli-ka-Mandir at Gwalior is exceptional, while Bateshwar and Amrol show related but varied forms. “Pratihara style” is an art-historical family resemblance, not proof that one king personally designed every chisel mark.

A tenth-century Malwa sandstone goddess in the British Museum is over a meter tall. Her lotus seat and powerful divine body belonged to a carefully carved sacred image, not an ordinary portrait. Museum labels can locate style and material, but missing excavation context limits what one sculpture says about its first worshippers.

A central Indian Gauri sculpture places Ganesha on a lotus in the goddess’s hand and an iguana-like creature near her feet; smaller women are interpreted as donors. Divine family imagery and human patrons meet in one object, but elite religious sculpture cannot serve as a candid photograph of everybody’s clothes or home.

The 876 Gwalior inscription writes small circular zeros in 270 and 50 while measuring a flower garden and its daily garlands. Zero was doing practical paperwork, not posing alone on a chalkboard. The record is famous because its date and place are secure, though Indian place-value notation had a longer history.

sections.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice

items.text: Court poet Rajashekhara served Mahendrapala, and his wife Avantisundari was credited with opinions on literary criticism that he quoted. This learned couple offers rare evidence for an elite woman’s intellectual work. It cannot prove that girls of every caste or village had equal access to books and teachers.

Early medieval society combined Brahmanical varna ideals with many regionally specific jatis, occupations and status claims. Landholding, court service, craft, gender and ritual rank shaped opportunity. Sources written by elite men describe hierarchy more clearly than children, servants or laborers speaking in their own voices, so certainty is uneven.

Written sample, in readable modern Devanagari normalization: “ॐ स्वस्ति । श्रीप्रयागसमीपगङ्गातटावासे ... श्रीमत्त्रिलोचनपालदेवः”. The 1027 Jhusi plate is Sanskrit in Nagari characters, while an earlier Gwalior record uses Siddhamatrika. This display regularizes the editor’s Roman text; it is not a facsimile of the copper letters or their original spacing.

Transliteration: “oṁ svasti | śrī-prayāga-samīpa-gaṅgā-taṭāvāse ... śrīmat-trilocanapāladevaḥ”. Translation: “Om. Fortune! Residing on the bank of the Ganges near illustrious Prayaga ... the illustrious Trilochanapala.” The ellipsis skips royal genealogy, so the sample is an opening fragment, not a complete sentence. It locates the issuing court before naming its ruler.

Convention links the plate to late Kannauj Pratiharas because it names Vijayapala, Rajyapala and Trilochanapala, but its first editor noted that no dynasty is named. This teaches real evidence with a real limit: genealogy alone does not erase doubt for historians.

sections.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off

items.text: At Anai in the middle Ganges plain, a 700 to 1000 layer preserved a mud house, ovens, red-ware cooking pots, storage jars, spouted vessels, iron objects, glass bangles, cowries and miniature vessels. This nearby settlement is regional comparison, not proof that every Pratihara household owned the same objects.

Possible meals drew on wheat or barley flatbreads and porridge, rice where water allowed, millets, pulses, oils, sugarcane products, fruit, vegetables and dairy or meat according to place, wealth and custom. Crop lists cannot reconstruct a fixed menu, and feast food was not the same as a laborer’s everyday bowl.

Stone deities and donors wear jewelry, arranged hair and draped garments that display sculptors’ ideals and elite presentation. Cotton cultivation and craft records support textile production, but cloth rarely survives in the region’s soil. The safest clothing picture combines fibers, tools and images while admitting that colors and everyday patches are mostly lost.

Markets brought cultivators, oil pressers, potters, metalworkers, cloth sellers, carriers, money handlers and animal dealers into exchange. Pehowa’s horse merchants show that traders could organize collective payments. A child might see impressive horses there, but no source says every market was a permanent fairground.

Rajashekhara imagined an aspiring poet reading and writing in the morning, discussing poetry after lunch and socializing in the evening. It is elite advice, not an average timetable. Songs, stories and performance surely mattered, but the consulted Pratihara evidence does not securely identify a particular children’s board game or toy.

sections.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued

items.text: The wider Susruta tradition discusses anatomy, surgery, medicines and learning from a teacher, but its textual layers and dates are debated. It gives Indian medical background rather than a patient chart from Kannauj. Household caregivers, herbal specialists and learned physicians probably served people unequally, yet direct Pratihara clinic evidence is sparse.

Early medieval learning included mathematics, astronomy, medical and technical texts, while craftspeople also learned through practiced work. The written zero, precise stone cutting and irrigation records show skills in action. A surviving achievement does not reveal one universal school system; most children probably learned duties within households and occupations.

Jhusi’s archaeological list records a tank and deep stone-lined wells at a settlement beside the Ganges. Those structures supplied water that could serve drinking, ritual, washing or bathing, but the source does not assign every use. Nor does it tell us how often each person washed or how clean the water remained.

The Anai report describes a mud house, ovens, vessels and nearby wells but no securely identified household latrine in its 700 to 1000 layer. The directly Pratihara records consulted here are equally silent. Wells, drains, pits or ring structures must not be renamed toilets without archaeological evidence; sanitation probably varied household by household.

The Pratihara court dissolved around the 1030s, but fields, waterworks, temples, craft knowledge, Sanskrit record keeping and local communities continued under other rulers. The atlas keeps the id until 1200 and then redraws the region again. Political endings change institutions and risks; they do not switch ordinary life off like a lamp.

ending.text: Around 1036, the last possible inscriptional trace of a Pratihara ruler appears at Kara, although Yashapala’s connection to the imperial family is disputed. The Kannauj-centered empire had already broken apart, and no continuous Pratihara state can be demonstrated through the atlas endpoint of 1200. Chandelas, Kalachuris, Gahadavalas, Chauhans, Palas, Paramaras and other powers shaped different parts of the old political world. Farms, markets, temples, waterworks, crafts and families continued under those changing authorities. This card therefore ends the polity around the 1030s, leaves structured successors empty rather than inventing one heir, and treats the remaining atlas interval as a documented map error and afterlife.
